ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, an isosceles triangle with a vertex angle of $36^\circ$ and the ratio of its base to its legs equal to $k$ is known as a golden triangle. Given that the leg $AB=1$ in the $\triangle ABC$ which is the first golden triangle, $\triangle BCD$ is the second golden triangle, and $\triangle CDE$ is the third golden triangle, and so on, what is the perimeter of the third golden triangle?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Since $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle BCD$ are both isosceles triangles with a vertex angle of $36^\circ$,
\[
\therefore \triangle ABC \sim \triangle BCD,
\]
\[
\therefore \text{the perimeter of } \triangle BCD : \text{the perimeter of } \triangle ABC = BC: AB,
\]
Given that $AB=AC=1$, and $\frac{BC}{AB}=k$,
\[
\therefore BC=k,
\]
\[
\therefore \text{the perimeter of } \triangle ABC = AB+AC+BC=2+k,
\]
\[
\therefore \text{the perimeter of } \triangle BCD : \text{the perimeter of } \triangle ABC = k,
\]
\[
\therefore \text{the perimeter of } \triangle BCD = k(2+k),
\]
By the same reasoning, \text{the perimeter of } $\triangle CDE$ : \text{the perimeter of } $\triangle BCD = k$,
\[
\therefore \text{the perimeter of } \triangle CDE = k^2(2+k) = \boxed{k^2(2+k)}.
\]

raw_record.original_question: As shown in the figure, an isosceles triangle with a vertex angle of $36^\circ$ and the ratio of its base to its legs equal to $k$ is known as a golden triangle. Given that the leg $AB=1$ in $\triangle ABC$, which is the first golden triangle, $\triangle BCD$ is the second golden triangle, and $\triangle CDE$ is the third golden triangle. What is the perimeter of the third golden triangle?
raw_record.answer:
\textbf{Solution:} Since $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle BCD$ are both isosceles triangles with a vertex angle of $36^\circ$,
\[
\therefore \triangle ABC \sim \triangle BCD,
\]
\[
\therefore \text{the perimeter of } \triangle BCD : \text{the perimeter of } \triangle ABC = BC: AB,
\]
Given that $AB=AC=1$, and $\frac{BC}{AB}=k$,
\[
\therefore BC=k,
\]
\[
\therefore \text{the perimeter of } \triangle ABC = AB+AC+BC=2+k,
\]
\[
\therefore \text{the perimeter of } \triangle BCD : \text{the perimeter of } \triangle ABC = k,
\]
\[
\therefore \text{the perimeter of } \triangle BCD = k(2+k),
\]
By the same reasoning, \text{the perimeter of } \triangle CDE : \text{the perimeter of } \triangle BCD = k,
\[
\therefore \text{the perimeter of } \triangle CDE = k^2(2+k) = \boxed{k^2(2+k)}.
\]
raw_record.final_cot: First describe the image: in the figure, the outer large triangle is ABC, A is above, B is at the lower left, and C is at the lower right; inside there is triangle BCD, which shares side BC with the outer triangle; further inside there is triangle CDE, which shares side CD with the second triangle. Points E and F are also marked in the figure, among which the third golden triangle corresponds to CDE. Then reason: the problem states that ABC, BCD, and CDE are all golden triangles, that is, they are all isosceles triangles with vertex angle 36°, and the ratio of the base to the waist is k, so these three triangles have the same shape and are similar to one another. In the first golden triangle ABC, AB=1, and AB and AC are the waists, so AC=1; the ratio of base BC to waist AB is k, so BC=k. Thus P(ABC)=AB+AC+BC=1+1+k=2+k. From the structure in the figure, BC is a waist of the second golden triangle BCD, so the similarity enlargement factor from ABC to BCD is BC/AB=k, so P(BCD)=kP(ABC)=k(2+k). Similarly, CD is the base of the second golden triangle BCD and serves as a waist of the third golden triangle CDE, so the similarity factor from BCD to CDE is still k. Therefore P(CDE)=kP(BCD)=k^2(2+k).
